o: Count integers in [low, high] (given as decimal strings, up to 100 digits!) whose adjacent digits differ by exactly 1 — e.g., 123, 987, 10. In [1,11] all of 1..10 qualify (10 numbers); in [90,101] only 98 and 101. Since numbers have up to 100 digits we cannot iterate; use digit DP: count stepping numbers ≤ X, answer = f(high) − f(low) + [low is stepping]. States: position, previous digit, tight flag, and whether we've started the number (leading zeros mean shorter numbers, whose digits are unconstrained by a predecessor).
k: Digit DP over the decimal string with state (pos, prevDigit, tight, started).
Leading zeros = building a shorter number; while not started, any nonzero digit may begin freely.
Answer = f(high) − f(low) + indicator(low itself is a stepping number).

a.i: f(X) counts stepping numbers in [1, X]. At each position, if not yet started, we may place a 0 (stay unstarted) or any digit d (start, prev=d); if started, next digit must be prev±1 and ≤ tight bound. Memoize on (pos, prev, tight, started); tight=true paths are visited once per branch so caching is safe.
s: Add 1 if low is itself a stepping number.
a.t: O(L · 10 · 2 · 2) ≈ O(L) states with 10 transitions each, L = digit length ≤ 100.

w: Digit DP is the only viable tool here — never convert the strings to numbers. Pitfalls: forgetting the f(low) exclusion (subtract, then re-add if low itself steps), mishandling leading zeros (the 'started' flag), and negative intermediate results modulo. Follow-up: count stepping numbers in a range without string bounds (BFS over 0..high numerically), or generalize to adjacent difference ≤ k.
